It refused the newly raised permissive-possession plea because it was a late factual plea, inconsistent with the earlier pleading, not tested below, and likely prejudicial; it also rejected any presumption of permission from family relationship alone.

historical_target.decisive_reason: The Court found that the appellant had put United Automobiles in possession and thereby parted with possession; United Automobiles was a separate entity, not a licensee or possessor on the appellant's behalf, and the fixed rent supported the conclusion that a sub-lease had been created. The Court then gave two independent reasons why the lease clause could not save the appellant: the sub-letting-permission term in the unregistered lease deed was inadmissible with the lease, and, alternatively, the clause was only general consent rather than landlord consent in writing to the specific sub-letting to United Automobiles.

The irresist- ible conclusion is that the appellant has created a sub- lease in favour of its dealer.
the appellant can not, in the present circumstances, be allowed to rely upon the clause in his unregistered lease deed.

historical_target.disposition: Civil Appeals 387 and 388 of 2004 dismissed with costs; the appellant in Civil Appeal 387 was granted three months to vacate subject to undertaking.
historical_target.decisive_reason: The Court held that the transferor's tenancy/occupancy rights vested in the Indian transferee, the American transferor ceased to exist from the appointed day, and the Indian Company thereafter occupied the premises. Section 14(1)(b) was held to contain no exception merely because the amalgamation was court-sanctioned or pursued to comply with law. The appellant could not treat the American Company as extinct for FERA yet still existing for rent-control possession. Civil Appeal 388 also had the additional procedural point that the American Company had not filed a Second Appeal in the High Court, and in any event raised the same rejected grounds.

evidence.quote: the original lessee, namely, the American Company ceased to exist with effect from the Appointed Day i.e. 1.1.1982 and thereafter the Indian Company came in possession and is in occupation of the premises in dispute.
the Act does not make any exception in favour of a lessee who may have adopted such a course of action in order to secure compliance of law.
the inescapable conclusion is that it is the Indian Company which is in occupation and is carrying on business in the premises in question rendering the appellant liable for eviction.
Civil Appeal No. 387 of 2004 and Civil Appeal No. 388 of 2004 are dismissed with costs.
The American Company did not challenge the order of the Rent Control Tribunal by filing a Second Appeal in the High Court.
